items.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I was performing Charles Mingus’ “Meditations on Integration.” ... I wonder if the music’s going to sound like that. I mean like how Duke Ellington and Charles Mingus, you know they would change from meter to meter

ctx.x: That’s great. I’ve heard some fascinating Chinese music that’s basically just percussion and cymbals. Great stuff. Have you adapted any of that kind of —

Well that’s a great question because I find that the future in Chinese music, putting aside Paul Robeson and I agree with him, said that the greatest contribution from China — well he actually said the Orient — but in China, was its melodic development. But there is like what I discovered when I was in Beijing in 1994 and I was there studying Beijing opera percussion or Beijing opera music and I met with a couple of Chinese musicians in the Beijing opera, and one of them was a percussionist, I learned of like…

exposed to some rhythmic organizations. Like they have these four gongs and they’re pitched differently. And I don’t want to get into the technical aspect of it, but one was like they go [scats beat] and then all of a sudden they go into this what they call the horse leg rhythm or mater. So actually you can visually think of it, so they go [scats beats]. And when I heard that I was performing Charles Mingus’ “Meditations on Integration.” And they had this rhythm that [scats] and I could hear that melody going…
